tip: 'göre' (according to) takes the dative: 'dedeme göre' (according to my grandfather) adds -e to 'dedem'.
'bitirirsen' ends in -sen, the if-you form: if you finish this task. The main clause then states the result.
Turkish marks than with the ablative -dan, not a separate word: 'Ankara'dan daha büyük' (bigger than Ankara).
Passive here adds -il to the stem: 'gönderdi' (sent) becomes 'gönderildi' (was sent), with no doer named.
-den dolayı means because of, and needs the ablative -den first: 'gürültü' becomes 'gürültüden dolayı' (because of the noise).
Causative -ir makes someone do the act: 'içti' (drank) becomes 'içirdi' (made take), and the taker goes dative: 'hastaya'.
To report a thought, -dığını turns the verb into a noun object: 'anlamadığını söyledi' = said that he did not understand it.
-madan önce means before doing something: 'kararmak' (to darken) becomes 'kararmadan önce' (before it got dark).
-mıştım is the past before the past: 'sıkıldım' (I got bored) becomes 'sıkılmıştım' (I had gotten bored) for an earlier state.
'ceza yemek' literally is to eat a fine, the normal way to say get fined: 'trafik cezası yedim' = I got a traffic fine.
'ilgilenmek' (to tend, take care of) pairs with -yle: 'bahçe' becomes 'bahçeyle ilgilendi' (took care of the garden).
In a passive, the doer gets 'tarafından' (by): 'annem tarafından hazırlandı' = were prepared by my mother.
-dığında means when something happened: 'yağmak' (to fall) becomes 'yağdığında' (when it snowed).
Proper nouns split off case suffixes with an apostrophe: 'İstanbul'a' (to Istanbul), never written 'Istanbula'.
A specific, definite object takes the accusative -u: 'form' becomes 'formu' (the particular form) as the thing acted on.
'unutmak' takes a verb turned into a noun with -mayı: 'sulamak' (to water) becomes 'sulamayı unuttum' (I forgot to water).
Past unreal condition: -saydık sets the if, -irdik the result: 'çıksaydık' then 'yetişirdik' = had we left, we would have caught it.
Written as its own word, 'da' means also or too: 'sağlığını da ihmal etme' = do not neglect your health either.
'sen' becomes 'sana' in the dative, an irregular form (not 'sene'): 'sana' then 'söyleyeceğim' = I will tell you.
-erdik marks a repeated past habit: 'çizmek' (to draw) becomes 'çizerdik' (we used to draw).
The -ebil in 'gelebilirsin' adds can or able to: 'gel' (come) plus ebil plus ir plus sin means you are able to come.
The -mış in 'çıkmamış' marks hearsay: she has apparently never gone abroad, something you did not witness yourself.
The passive lives inside the verb: 'duy' (hear) plus ul gives 'duyuldu', it was heard, with no doer named.
Add -ınca to a verb for once or when: 'ısın' (warm up) plus ınca gives 'ısınınca', once it warmed up.
The -meli in 'gitmeliyim' means must or have to: 'git' (go) plus meli plus yim, I must go.
'katılmak' (to agree with) takes the dative, so the person ends in -e: 'size katılıyorum', I agree with you.
'rağmen' means despite and needs the dative before it: 'olmasına rağmen', despite its being, so despite the cold.
For an unreal past pair -saydı with -mazdı: 'olsaydım', had I been, plus 'olmazdı', would not have happened.
'o kadar' with 'ki' frames a result, so much that: 'o kadar çok çalıştım ki' means I worked so much that my eyes are closing.
For no matter how, repeat the verb: the -ırsan if-form then the bare command: 'çalışırsan çalış', however much you work.
